results.title: ε, A Nuisance No More | Zack Nado
results.content: One reason why the effects of ε may not have been noticed much in popular optimizers such as Adam and RMSProp is because they use a square root around their second moment estimates of the gradients, which can be viewed as a non-linear version of damping; once the numerics of dividing by zero have been solved by ε, the square root can handle diminishinig large dimensions and increasing small ones, which will have a similar normalizing effect on the eigenvalues. Therefore, **it may be useful to jointly tune of ε and weight decay, beyond the effect that they both have on the effective learning rate of an update.**. While I agree with a lot of the existing literature[18] on tuning the learning rate and learning rate schedule first, I also believe that if you can afford it, when tuning optimizers trying one or two values of ε that is a few orders of magnitude larger than the default can be useful.

results.title: Choosing Data Visualization Libraries: Expressivity vs Efficiency | by Kelvin Li | Medium
results.content: # Choosing Data Visualization Libraries: Expressivity vs Efficiency. To create data visualizations, many libraries are available to application developers. Choosing the right visualization library is important. Different types of visualization libraries provide different levels of expressivity and efficiency. There are three main types of visualization libraries: 1) Chart Templates, 2) Declarative Grammars, and 3) Graphics APIs. To understand their key differences, the data visualization pipeline is useful. ### Data Visualization Pipeline. The operations involved in data visualization typically include:. * Visual Mapping — map data attributes to visual channels (e.g., color, size, position, type of mark) to create visual elements from data structures. The three types of visualization libraries provide different levels of support for these operations as shown here. A common type of visualization library uses pre-defined chart templates (e.g. bar, line, and area charts) with a fixed input data format. Since chart templates are used, the visual mapping operations are also limited but allowed some customization. Therefore, a visualization library with chart templates requires low programming effort but provides low expressivity. To provide better expressivity for authoring visualizations, a declarative visualization grammar can be used to describe how data attributes should be mapped to visual channels (e.g., color, size, position, type of mark) for generating visualizations. ### Graphics APIs. This type of library provides more control of the visual elements in visualizations by allowing programmers to perform computer graphics operations. Utility and wrapper libraries can be built on top of a visualization library of graphic API for boosting efficiency and productivity. For example, D3.js offers a suite of utilities to leverage SVG for creating visualizations, which makes it more like a declarative grammar but with more expressivity for rendering. For explanative tasks (e.g. explorative data analysis), it would be better to use common visualization types, like bar charts and scatter plots. Therefore, chart templates or declarative visualization libraries are good choices here. Moreover, developers can choose two different libraries in one application — use chart templates for explorative applications and declarative grammar for explanative applications. I hope that my classification and explanation of different types of visualization libraries can help application developers to effectively choose the right libraries for visualization.
